args.body:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

TO: Litigation Partners; Litigation Associates
FROM: Litigation Dispute Resolution Team
DATE: January 2026
RE: Opposition Issues Memorandum — Motion to Dismiss
MATTER: litigation-dispute-resolution analyze — Analyze Counterparty Motion to Dismiss (Issue Identification Memorandum)

I. INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE

This memorandum analyzes the counterparty's motion to dismiss (the "Motion") as against the operative complaint, Master Services Agreement ("MSA"), supporting declaration, and deal-team correspondence. The purpose of this memorandum is to (a) identify every substantive deviation the counterparty introduced in the Motion relative to the base materials, (b) reconcile each deviation against the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and (c) set forth recommended opposition positions consistent with the client's controlling priorities.

The base operating materials consist of the following:
- The complaint and underlying claims;
- The Master Services Agreement (MSA) and its scheduled exhibits;
- The witness/declaration submitted in support of the Motion;
- The deal-team correspondence governing analysis priorities.

The counterparty's markup of the MSA introduces deviations in three principal areas: (i) indemnification (cap and basket structure), (ii) the Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") definition, and (iii) the survival period / limitation period for core representations. Each deviation is analyzed below against the base materials and the controlling schedules. In addition, the matter folder contained a misfiled administrative correspondence file (Administrative File 21) that concerns an unrelated client engagement. That file was expressly identified as a distractor and is NOT relied upon in this analysis.

II. CONTROLLING ANALYSIS PRIORITIES

The controlling deal-team correspondence (latest message on the thread) instructs that the client will (a) concede the conversion of the indemnification basket from a deductible basket to a tipping basket, but (b) treat any reduction to the survival period for core representations as a walk-away issue. Earlier messages that stated the opposite priority ordering are superseded and do not control. This memorandum therefore treats the survival-period concession as non-negotiable and the basket conversion as a ceded point for strategic purposes, while continuing to press every other objection raised by the base materials and schedules.

III. DEVIATION 1 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP REDUCTION AND BASKET CONVERSION

A. The Counterparty's Deviation

The counterparty's Motion effects two changes to the indemnification framework. First, the indemnification cap is silently reduced from the amount agreed in the MSA base materials. Second, the basket is converted from a deductible basket to a tipping basket. The combined effect of these changes is to reduce the counterparty's net exposure: a lower cap truncates the ceiling on recovery, while conversion to a tipping basket means that, once the threshold is crossed, the full amount of loss (not merely the excess over the basket) becomes recoverable.

B. Reconciliation Against Base Materials and Schedules

The base MSA materials establish the indemnification cap and basket structure as negotiated terms. Nothing in the operative agreement authorized a unilateral reduction of the cap. The client has addressed the basket conversion as a ceded point in the controlling correspondence and will not oppose that conversion as a threshold matter. The cap reduction, however, is distinct and must be opposed.

Schedule 5.2 of the MSA lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. The scheduled exceptions narrow the seller's/respondent's representation regarding the liabilities retained by the counterparty. If the cap is reduced and the basket converted without correspondingly adjusting the Schedule 5.2 liabilities, the result is that liabilities that the parties allocated to the counterparty under the schedules are effectively offloaded back onto the client. The schedules control over any general statements in the base materials to the contrary.

C. Recommended Opposition Position

The client should oppose the cap reduction on multiple grounds:
1. The cap reduction is a unilateral modification of a negotiated term with no contractual basis in the MSA.
2. Schedule 5.2 retained-liability allocations presuppose the original cap; reducing the cap without revising Schedule 5.2 shifts economic risk in a manner inconsistent with the parties' allocation bargain.
3. The cap reduction is not among the deviations the client has conceded, and it materially alters the risk profile of the transaction.

Consistent with the controlling instruction, the basket conversion should not be separately opposed. However, the opposition memorandum should note that the client is agreeing to the basket conversion only in the form reflected in the base materials' schedules and will not accept any further erosion of the indemnification structure.

IV. DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT CARVE-OUTS

A. The Counterparty's Deviation

The counterparty's Motion adds new carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter." This tracks directly onto two pending regulatory inquiries that form the factual backdrop of the litigation.

B. Reconciliation Against Base Materials and Schedules

Schedule 3.7 of the MSA discloses two pending regulatory inquiries. These inquiries intersect the markup's MAE carve-outs directly: the carve-outs are drafted to exclude from the MAE definition precisely the regulatory actions that arise from those two pending inquiries. The base MSA materials define MAE in terms that do not include a carve-out for regulatory action of this character. The counterparty's addition seeks to immunize itself from MAE-based consequences arising from these pre-existing inquiries.

The scheduled exceptions in Schedule 3.7 control over general statements in the base materials. Because the two pending inquiries were disclosed on Schedule 3.7, they were known, quantified, and allocated risk at signing. The counterparty cannot now re-characterize those known items as MAE carve-outs to avoid the consequences of the MAE definition that were already negotiated with the disclosed inquiries in view.

C. Recommended Opposition Position

The client should oppose the MAE carve-outs on the following bases:
1. The carve-outs retroactively dilute a negotiated definition to shield the counterparty from consequences of regulatory action that was disclosed and considered at signing (Schedule 3.7).
2. Allowing the carve-outs would strip the MAE clause of its protective function with respect to known regulatory exposures, which is precisely the kind of risk the MSA was designed to allocate.
3. The carve-outs conflict with the scheduled exceptions, which control under the MSA.
4. The addition of these carve-outs in a dismissal motion is an attempt to change the substantive contractual standard governing the dispute, not merely to resolve procedural issues.

V. DEVIATION 3 — LIMITATION PERIOD REDUCTION (SURVIVAL PERIOD)

A. The Counterparty's Deviation

The counterparty's Motion introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival of the core representations. This directly contradicts Exhibit B of the MSA, which sets the survival matrix for the representations.

B. Reconciliation Against Base Materials and Schedules

Exhibit B establishes the survival matrix that governs how long each category of representation survives after closing. The counterparty's limitation-period change contradicts the survival framework set forth in Exhibit B. Because Exhibit B is an agreed schedule of the MSA, it controls over the counterparty's unilateral revision attempt.

This deviation is of critical importance given the controlling client instruction: **any survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue**. The client treats the survival period terms as a non-negotiable condition. The counterparty's attempt to shorten survival for core representations therefore strikes at a term the client has identified as a deal-breaker.

C. Recommended Opposition Position

The client should treat this issue as a walk-away matter and oppose it in the strongest terms:
1. The survival period for core representations is a central negotiated term memorialized in Exhibit B.
2. The counterparty's attempt to shorten survival is a wholesale revision of the survival matrix, not a minor markup.
3. Per the controlling deal-team instruction, any survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue — the client will not proceed if this deviation is not resolved.
4. The opposition should demand the survival matrix remain exactly as set forth in Exhibit B, with no reduction for any core representation.

VI. RECONCILIATION OF DEVIATIONS AGAINST THE SCHEDULES AND DISCLOSURES

The schedules and exhibits exercise controlling force over the base materials as follows:

- Schedule 3.7 (pending regulatory inquiries) intersects the MAE carve-outs. The disclosed inquiries were known, allocated risk at signing, and cannot now be turned into carve-outs. The opposition should cite Schedule 3.7 to defeat the MAE carve-outs.

- Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities) intersects the indemnification changes. The markup's cap reduction would silently shift retained liabilities. The opposition should cite Schedule 5.2 to prevent the cap reduction from altering the pre-existing liability allocation.

- Exhibit B (survival matrix) contradicts the limitation-period change. Exhibit B controls the survival framework, and the counterparty's change must be rejected. The opposition should cite Exhibit B to defeat the survival-period reduction.

VII. SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDED POSITIONS

| Deviation | Client Position | Basis | 
|-----------|----------------|-------|
| Indemnification cap reduction | Oppose | No contractual basis; Schedule 5.2 retained-liability allocation presupposes original cap |
| Basket conversion (deductible → tipping) | Concede (per controlling instruction) | Client has agreed; do not separately oppose |
| MAE carve-outs for regulatory action | Oppose | Schedule 3.7 disclosures; carve-outs defeat protective function of MAE clause |
| Survival-period reduction for core reps | Walk-away / Oppose in strongest terms | Exhibit B survival matrix is controlling; client treats any reduction as non-negotiable |

VIII. ADDITIONAL OBSERVATIONS

The motion to dismiss must also be assessed for any procedural or pleading deficiencies that could independently defeat the Motion, including whether the Motion properly incorporates the MSA, exhibits, and declarations by reference and whether any factual assertions in the supporting declaration exceed the permissible scope.

The misfiled administrative correspondence (Administrative File 21) was reviewed and excluded from reliance. It relates to an unrelated client engagement and does not bear on this matter.

IX. CONCLUSION

The counterparty's motion to dismiss introduces four material deviations from the base materials: the indemnification cap reduction, basket conversion, MAE carve-outs, and survival-period reduction. Each must be reconciled against the controlling schedules and exhibits. The client has conceded the basket conversion but treats survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. The opposition should oppose the cap reduction, oppose the MAE carve-outs, and treat the survival-period reduction as a non-negotiable deal-breaker, in each case grounding the position in the controlling schedules (Schedule 3.7, Schedule 5.2, and Exhibit B).

Prepared by: Litigation Dispute Resolution Team
Status: Privileged and Confidential — Attorney Work Product
